chunks: They said: And a man from the people of As-Sawad stood up to him when he reached this point in his sermon,
he handed him a letter, and he began looking at it. When he finished reading it, Ibn 'Abbas said to him: O Commander of the Faithful, if only your speech had continued from where you stopped!
He replied (peace be upon him): Far off, O Ibn 'Abbas! That was a camel's roar that surged forth and then subsided!
Ibn 'Abbas said: By Allah, I never grieved over any speech as I grieved over that speech, that the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) did not reach it to the extent he wished.
ai.seo_question: What was the meaning of Ali's metaphor about the camel's roar in the Shqshaqiya sermon?
ai.summary: This poignant moment in the Shqshaqiya sermon highlights the tension between Ali's rhetorical mastery and the political realities of his time, as recorded by Sharif al-Radi. Ibn Abbas’s deep regret underscores the belief that Ali’s full exposition of his right to leadership was truncated by external interruptions, symbolized by the 'roar' that settled before reaching its climax. This incident serves as a key narrative device in Shia historiography to illustrate the suppression of Ali's voice during the early caliphate.

en.sayed-ali-raza: (It is said that when Amīr al-mu’minīn reached here in his sermon a man of Iraq stood up and handed him over a writing. Amīr al-mu’minīn began looking at it,
when Ibn ‘Abbās said, “O Amīr al-mu’minīn, I wish you resumed your Sermon from where you broke it.”
Thereupon he replied, “O Ibn ‘Abbās it was like the foam of a Camel which gushed out but subsided.”
Ibn ‘Abbās says that he never grieved over any utterance as he did over this one because Amīr al-mu’minīn could not finish it as he wished to.)
